title: Cardiologist Urges Earlier ECG Screening for At-Risk Patients as India's Heart Disease Burden Grows
excerpt: Dr. Vijay D'Silva says skipping early ECG screening costs lives — but U.S. guidelines add an important caveat: screening pays off for at-risk patients, not healthy low-risk adults.
body:
• Dr. Vijay D'Silva, Medical Director of White Lotus International Hospital, argues heart disease builds silently for years — and that skipping early heart screening costs lives.
  • A resting electrocardiogram takes only minutes and can detect abnormal rhythms, evidence of prior silent heart damage, and electrical conduction problems.
  • He urges earlier ECG screening for people with hypertension, diabetes, early family history of heart disease, smoking, obesity, abnormal cholesterol, chronic work stress, or unexplained fatigue and breathlessness.
  • Counterpoint: the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against routine ECG screening for asymptomatic low-risk adults, saying evidence is insufficient for intermediate and high-risk groups — so screening decisions should be based on a doctor's risk assessment.

The heart rarely fails overnight

The heart does not usually give up in a single night. The trouble quietly accumulates for years, hiding behind other illnesses, until it presents itself as chest pain or a heart attack. In India, where the share of cardiovascular disease among younger adults is increasing year by year, early diagnosis has become as important as cardiac prevention. That is the argument Dr. Vijay D'Silva, Medical Director of White Lotus International Hospital and Clinical Advisor and Mentor at Heartnet India, made in an interview with HealthShots, reported by Hindustan Times.

"There are multiple prevention tools. Of all the tools available to clinicians, none is more straightforward or more widely available than the ECG," Dr. D'Silva said. Yet, he added, it remains one of the most underutilised elements of preventive health care. The World Health Organisation notes that the majority of early cardiovascular disease can be prevented by managing modifiable risks — elevated blood pressure, smoking, poor diet, and physical inactivity.

Why you should not wait for symptoms

Heart disease develops silently. Rhythm problems, asymptomatic ischemia, and preclinical electrical disturbances can all exist long before a patient first feels anything wrong. "Many patients recognise that they are completely in good health until they suddenly require hospital admission for an established cardiac disease," Dr. D'Silva said. "Often, compared with cases diagnosed earlier and treated accordingly, treatment becomes more complex, more costly, and far more emotionally stressful."

The healthcare focus, he argued, must shift from treating people when they suffer an attack to screening for risk and intervening early. A simple ECG records the heart's electrical activity in a few minutes. It can detect abnormal heart rhythms, evidence of prior silent damage to the heart muscle, and problems with electrical signal conduction. An ECG alone cannot diagnose every heart condition, but it often serves as the first sign that leads to further investigation — long before symptoms appear.

"While an ECG takes only minutes, it can change the course of a person's cardiac future."

— Dr. Vijay D'Silva, Medical Director, White Lotus International Hospital

Who should consider earlier screening

Age alone should not decide who gets a heart check, Dr. D'Silva said — risk profile should. His high-risk categories: people with high blood pressure or diabetes, those with a family history of heart disease at a young age, smokers, the obese, those with abnormal cholesterol, professionals under constant pressure and long working hours, and anyone with unexplained tiredness and breathlessness. In all of these cases, an ECG should be part of prevention based on overall risk, not ordered only after a crisis.

An honest caveat: what the U.S. evidence says

Here a journalistic caveat is required, because Western guidelines draw a sharper line. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends against screening with resting or exercise ECG to predict cardiovascular events in asymptomatic adults at low risk — a D recommendation — concluding with moderate certainty that potential harms (unnecessary invasive procedures, overtreatment, diagnostic mislabelling) equal or exceed potential benefits in that group. For asymptomatic adults at intermediate or high risk, the Task Force says the evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms — an I statement. The Task Force did note that adults at intermediate risk have the greatest potential for net benefit from screening, and its clinical considerations allow screening where it changes management in higher-risk patients.

That nuance does not contradict Dr. D'Silva so much as refine him: the case for ECG screening is strongest exactly in the at-risk groups he names, and weakest in healthy low-risk adults with no risk factors. Screening should follow a doctor's risk assessment, not a blanket schedule for everyone.

Taking the ECG beyond hospital walls

Technology is making early screening far more accessible. Portable ECG devices and digital tools that interpret readings quickly mean a heart check no longer has to happen inside a large hospital. "First-line screening often happens at primary care clinics and neighbourhood physicians, supported by digital tools that can transmit reports to a specialist for a faster opinion if needed," Dr. D'Silva said. That early referral matters especially outside large urban areas, where reaching a cardiologist can take days or weeks — a delay that can significantly affect how a condition develops.

The diaspora angle: family history follows across borders

For the Indian diaspora, the family-history clause carries special weight. South Asians develop coronary artery disease at younger ages and carry a higher burden of cardiometabolic risk factors, so a father or uncle's early heart attack is not just a family story — it changes your own risk profile and the threshold at which screening makes sense. NRIs with that history, diabetes, or hypertension should raise ECG screening explicitly at their annual physical rather than assuming a standard blood panel covers it.

What to do with this information

The most useful change is simple: have a heart check before symptoms force one. For those already at risk, an ECG as part of a regular health check should become as routine as blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol checks. Broader awareness of early screening as a habit — not an emergency response — is what turns a minutes-long test into a genuinely life-changing intervention.
